key_insight: Higher urinary cadmium was associated with shorter conditional survival, with the largest absolute difference at the earliest survival-time percentile.
clinical_relevance: The findings support population-level efforts to reduce cadmium exposure but do not establish causality or guide individual treatment.
method: Linked NHANES 1999–2014 data for 24,338 US adults aged ≥40 to mortality records through 2019.
Used weighted censored quantile regression to estimate adjusted associations at the 10th, 25th, and 50th survival-time percentiles.
Examined blood lead and mercury and urinary cadmium and arsenic.
evidence_signal: Among 7,061 participants in the cadmium analysis, doubling urinary cadmium was associated with 1.71–1.92 years shorter conditional survival at the 10th percentile and 1.35–1.53 years shorter at the median.
watch_item: This observational environmental-exposure study—not AI cancer drug discovery research—cannot rule out residual confounding, and some median estimates were not estimable.
paper_title: Environmental toxic metal exposure and conditional mortality survival among US adults: a prospective cohort study
